intro: This branch builds a toolkit of basic graph shapes and the moves that change them: sliding, flipping and stretching. Knowing these lets a learner sketch and understand a new function quickly instead of plotting point by point.

IV.9.01.what: Getting to know the parent functions: the basic graph shapes, like the straight line and the U-shaped parabola, that others are built from.

levels.a: Recognizes the straight line, parabola and cubic (S-shaped) graphs.
levels.b: Recognizes the square root, V-shaped absolute value and reciprocal (one over x) graphs.
levels.c: Recognizes exponential (rapid growth) and logarithm (slow growth) graphs.
levels.d: Matches each graph to its equation.
levels.e: Recognizes a basic function written in an unfamiliar way.
levels.f: Counts how many times two basic graphs cross by picturing them.

IV.9.02.what: Sliding a graph up or down by adding or subtracting a number to the whole function.

levels.a: Sees that adding a number moves every point of the graph up by that amount.
levels.b: Tells whether a graph has moved up or down.
levels.d: Writes the equation of a shifted graph.

IV.9.03.what: Sliding a graph left or right by changing the input, which moves it the opposite way to the sign.

levels.a: Finds the new center of a graph shifted sideways.
levels.b: Explains why subtracting inside the bracket moves the graph right.
levels.d: Writes the equation of a graph shifted sideways.
levels.e: Spots a hidden sideways shift in an expanded equation.
levels.f: Shifts a graph until it is symmetric about the vertical axis.

IV.9.04.what: Flipping a graph in the x-axis (upside down) or the y-axis (left to right).

levels.a: Flips a point upside down by changing the sign of its height.
levels.b: Flips a point left to right by changing the sign of its x.
levels.d: Identifies which flip an equation shows.

IV.9.05.what: Stretching or squashing a graph vertically by multiplying the whole function by a number.

levels.a: Multiplies each point's height by the stretch number.
levels.b: Tells a stretch (number above 1) from a squash (number between 0 and 1).
levels.c: Tracks how key points like zeros and turning points move.
levels.d: Writes the equation of a stretched graph.
levels.e: Chooses a stretch so the graph reaches a target value.
levels.f: Finds the points that a vertical stretch leaves in place.

IV.9.06.what: Stretching or squashing a graph sideways by multiplying the input by a number.

levels.a: Divides each point's x by the number, bringing points closer to the axis.
levels.b: Sees that multiplying the input by 2 squashes the graph to half width.
levels.c: Tracks how zeros and turning points move sideways.
levels.d: Writes the equation of a sideways-stretched graph.

IV.9.07.what: Combining several moves, like a shift, a flip and a stretch, and doing them in the right order.

levels.a: Applies a stretch and a shift to a point, in the correct order.
levels.b: Tracks key points through several moves.
levels.c: Picks the graph of a fully transformed function.
levels.d: Describes a set of moves in words.

IV.9.08.what: Recognizing even functions (mirror-symmetric left to right) and odd functions (unchanged by a half-turn about the center).

levels.a: Uses the fact that an even function gives the same output for x and minus x.
levels.b: Uses the fact that an odd function gives opposite outputs for x and minus x.
levels.c: Tests a formula to see whether it is even or odd.
levels.e: Finds a value that makes a function even or odd.
levels.f: Separates off the odd part of a function to find an unknown output.

IV.9.09.what: Using symmetry to find more points on a graph and complete a sketch.

levels.a: Finds a mirror point for a graph symmetric about the vertical axis.
levels.b: Finds the matching point for a graph symmetric through the center point.
levels.c: Finds other mirror lines, such as through the tip of a V.
levels.d: Uses symmetry to complete half a graph.
levels.e: Finds a mirror point through a center other than the origin.
levels.f: Sees that two mirror lines force the graph to repeat.

IV.9.10.what: Describing end behavior: what a graph does far to the left and far to the right.

levels.a: Reads arrow notation describing where a graph heads.
levels.b: Describes the ends of a polynomial from its highest power.
levels.c: Reads the end behavior from a graph.
levels.d: Works out the end behavior from an equation in brackets.

IV.9.11.what: Understanding continuity informally: whether a graph can be drawn without lifting the pencil.

levels.a: Tells whether a graph can be drawn in one stroke.
levels.b: Measures the size of a jump between two pieces.
levels.c: Finds a hole, a single missing point.
levels.d: Finds where a graph breaks at a hole or at an asymptote (a line the graph approaches).

IV.9.12.what: Understanding asymptotes informally: lines a graph gets closer and closer to without reaching.

levels.a: Finds a vertical asymptote, where the graph shoots up or down.
levels.b: Finds a horizontal asymptote, the height the graph levels off at.
levels.c: Reads both kinds from a graph.
levels.d: Explains an asymptote in context, such as the lowest average cost per item.

IV.9.13.what: Using graphs to see whether a function can be undone (is one-to-one) and to picture its inverse.

levels.a: Uses the rule that a flat line may cross a one-to-one graph only once.
levels.b: Picks the inverse's graph as the mirror image across the diagonal line.
levels.c: Swaps a point's coordinates to get a point on the inverse.
levels.d: Swaps the domain and range for the inverse.
levels.e: Finds an inverse value by spotting the input that gives it.
levels.f: Finds when a function is its own inverse.

IV.9.14.what: Restricting the domain: using only part of a graph so the function can be undone.

levels.a: Explains why part of a graph must be cut away to allow an inverse.
levels.b: Chooses half of a parabola that passes the one-crossing test.
levels.c: Finds the inverse on that half.
levels.d: Checks that a proposed inverse really undoes the function.

IV.9.15.what: Composing functions, feeding one output into another, using tables and graphs instead of formulas.

levels.a: Uses a table to apply one function, then another.
levels.b: Does the same by reading two graphs.
levels.c: Finds which inputs are allowed for the combined function.
levels.d: Uses composition in real situations, such as cost after hours of baking.
levels.e: Works backwards through a composition to find the input.
levels.f: Applies a function many times by finding the repeating cycle.

IV.9.16.what: Choosing a model for data: straight-line, quadratic or exponential, by looking at patterns in a table.

levels.a: Recognizes equal differences as a straight-line pattern.
levels.b: Recognizes equal second differences as a quadratic pattern.
levels.c: Recognizes equal ratios, repeated multiplying, as an exponential pattern.
levels.d: Chooses a model from a description of a real situation.

IV.9.17.what: Comparing growth: seeing that repeated multiplying (exponential) eventually beats any steady or power-based growth.

levels.a: Compares a straight-line and an exponential function at one point.
levels.b: Finds when exponential growth finally overtakes a steady one.
levels.c: Compares the two using a table.
levels.d: Compares the two using a graph.
levels.e: Finds the last crossing, after which the exponential stays ahead for good.
levels.f: Compares two enormous powers without calculating them.

IV.9.18.what: Graphing functions with absolute value (distance from zero) applied, which folds parts of a graph over.

levels.a: Flips the parts of a graph below the axis to above it.
levels.b: Replaces the left half of a graph with a mirror of the right half.
levels.c: Solves an equation using the folded graph.
levels.d: Combines folding with shifts and other moves.
levels.e: Counts solutions for different values of an unknown using the graph.
levels.f: Solves equations with absolute values inside absolute values.
